answer: The registration of title to every land parcel under the Act must be “in accordance with the cadastral map prepared for that purpose.” Applying that rule here, the parcel being brought under the title-registration system must have its registration of title follow the cadastral map prepared for that purpose.

The rule is that, on receipt of the certified copies of cadastral maps, the Commissioner of Title Settlement must “publish a Notice in the Gazette,” and that Notice must call for “any claimants to the land parcel specified in such Notice to submit their claims to him within a prescribed period from the date of publication of such Notice.” After claims are received in response to that Notice, the Commissioner must “cause an investigation to be conducted in order to determine the genuinness or otherwise of claims made in response to a Notice under section 12.”

Applied to the facts, since the Commissioner of Title Settlement has received certified copies of cadastral maps for an area, he must publish the Gazette Notice inviting claimants to submit claims within the prescribed period. Once claims are submitted, an investigation must be carried out to determine whether those claims are genuine or otherwise.

The Act provides two different procedures.

1. **Reference of disputed claims during investigations**: If, during the course of investigations, the Commissioner of Title Settlement forms the opinion that, because the claims are disputed, it would be more appropriate for the investigations to be carried out by the District Court, the Commissioner of Title Settlement **may refer such claims for investigation and determination to the District Court** having jurisdiction over the area where the land is situate. (node_id: 21-1998/section-21)

2. **Appeal by an aggrieved claimant**: Any claimant who is aggrieved by a **Declaration of the Commissioner of Title Settlement under section 14** may **prefer an appeal** against that declaration **within the prescribed period** to the District Court having jurisdiction over the area where the land parcel is situate. (node_id: 21-1998/section-22)

Applied to the facts: because the parties’ claims to the same land parcel are seriously disputed during the title investigation, the Commissioner may refer those claims to the District Court for investigation and determination. Separately, if one claimant is dissatisfied with a declaration made by the Commissioner, that claimant’s remedy is to appeal to the District Court within the prescribed period. The first procedure is a Commissioner-initiated referral during investigations; the second is a claimant-initiated appeal after a declaration.

The statutory rule is that, for land parcels registered under the Registration of Title Act, a person acquiring an interest is not entitled to that title or interest unless it is registered under the Act. Also, registered land or any interest in it may be transferred or dealt with only in accordance with the Act, and any disposition otherwise effected is void. An instrument pertaining to land executed in accordance with the Act takes effect only on registration of that instrument under the Act.

Applied here, Nimal executed an instrument purporting to transfer an interest in a land parcel registered under the Act, but the instrument was not registered. On the supplied provisions, the transferee did not acquire the interest from the private agreement alone, because the interest is not acquired unless registered, and the instrument does not take effect until registration. The unregistered disposition is therefore void.

Under section 48, “Except in accordance with the provisions of this Act, an instrument pertaining to the ownership of a land parcel registered under this Act, made in favour of two or more persons in common shall be void and shall not be registered under this Act.”

Applied here, the instrument purports to convey the land parcel to two purchasers “as owners in common.” On the supplied facts, that means the instrument is void and must not be registered, unless it is made in accordance with the Act. Because no such compliance is stated, the instrument is invalid and not registrable under the Registration of Title Act.

The rule is that, for lands or interests in land registered under the Registration of Title Act with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership, the Prescription Ordinance (Chapter 68) “shall not apply.” Likewise, for land parcels registered under that Act with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership, the Partition Act “shall not apply.”

Applied to the facts, the parcel is registered with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership, so neither the Prescription Ordinance nor the Partition Act applies to that parcel.

The governing rule is that, once the Superintendent of Surveys is satisfied that the condominium plan conforms to the Apartment Ownership Law, No. 11 of 1973 and the Registration of Title Act, he must certify the plan on behalf of the Surveyor-General and then: (a) file the original of the condominium plan after making a suitable reference on the cadastral map used for registration of title; and (b) forward the duplicate of the condominium plan and the application of the owner to the appropriate Registrar of Title. 

Then, if the Registrar of Title is satisfied that the application conforms to the same laws, he must: (a) file the duplicate of the condominium plan in the Parcels File; (b) open a new title register in the Register for each condominium parcel shown on the Condominium Plan and make suitable cross references in the register in which the land parcel is registered; (c) record in the Property Section that the land comprised therein consists only of common property; (d) record in the Encumbrances Section that registers in respect of condominium parcels have been opened; (e) inform the applicant that the condominium parcels have been registered and notify him of the reference numbers of the relevant registers; and (f) issue a Certificate of Title after recovery of the prescribed fees.

Applying those rules here, because the condominium plan has already been approved as conforming to the applicable laws, the Superintendent should certify it, file the original with the cadastral-map reference, and send the duplicate and the owner's application to the appropriate Registrar of Title. The Registrar should then carry out the filing, open the new title registers for each condominium parcel, make the required cross-references and records, notify the applicant, and issue the Certificate of Title after the prescribed fees are recovered.

The governing rule is: when a person dies intestate leaving a spouse, “the surviving spouse shall inherit one-half of the property” [15-1876/section-22]. “Subject to the right of the surviving spouse,” the order of inheritance is first “descendants” [15-1876/section-23]. As to descendants, “Children, grandchildren, and remoter descendants are preferent to all others in the estate of the parents”; “all the children take equally per capita,” but “the children or remoter issue of a deceased child take per stirpes or by representation” [15-1876/section-24].

Applied to these facts, the surviving spouse takes 1/2 of the estate. The remaining 1/2 goes to descendants. There is one living child, and the two grandchildren are the children of a predeceased child, so the descendants’ half is divided per stirpes into two branches: one branch for the living child and one branch for the predeceased child’s issue. Thus:
- surviving spouse = 1/2
- living child = 1/2 of the remaining 1/2 = 1/4
- grandchildren together = 1/2 of the remaining 1/2 = 1/4, split equally
- each grandchild = 1/4 ÷ 2 = 1/8

The governing rule is that “Every will made beyond the limits of Sri Lanka containing any devise or disposition of immovable property situate within Sri Lanka, which shall have been duly made and executed according to and in conformity with the forms and solemnities prescribed by the law of the country where the same shall have been so made and executed, by any person who by the law of such country or of Sri Lanka if competent to make a will, shall be valid and effectual to alienate and pass the property in any immovable property so devised or disposed of by any such testator.”

Applied here, the will was executed outside Sri Lanka, it disposes of immovable property situated in Sri Lanka, it complies with the formalities of the country where it was executed, and the testator was competent under that country’s law. On those facts, the will is valid and effectual to alienate and pass the Sri Lankan immovable property.

Before any precept or order for the service of notice or summons is issued in proceedings or an action for enforcing a right of pre-emption, proof must be furnished to the court of the registration of the proceedings or action as a lis pendens in accordance with the Registration of Documents Ordinance. [59-1947/section-10]

As proof of the plaintiff's bona fides, the court may in its discretion order the plaintiff to deposit the purchase amount set out in the notice given under section 5. [59-1947/section-11]

If the plaintiff defaults in depositing that amount within the period the court allows, or within further periods the court allows not exceeding three months in the aggregate, the plaintiff's action shall be struck off the roll of pending cases. [59-1947/section-11]

The governing rule is that “A mortgage of a part of a tea or rubber estate as a divided lot shall, if it is effected on or after the appointed day, be null and void notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any other law.” The “appointed day” is “the eleventh day of December, 1957.”

Applied to the facts, the owner mortgages “a physically divided portion of that estate as a separate lot” after the appointed day. That is a mortgage of part of a tea estate as a divided lot, effected on or after the appointed day. Therefore, the mortgage is null and void under the Act.

No. The statute says that “No share in the common elements of a registered, Condominium Property or of a registered Semi Condominium Property shall be disposed of or otherwise dealt with except as appurtenant to a condominium parcel of such property.” So the share in the common elements cannot be sold or otherwise dealt with separately from the condominium parcel.

It also says that “any alienation of any condominium parcel shall be deemed also to convey the undivided share of the owner in the common elements appertaining to that condominium parcel notwithstanding the fact that no specific or particular reference has been made thereto in the instrument or deed relating to such alienation.” So if the condominium parcel itself is transferred, the attached undivided share in the common elements is transferred with it automatically, even if the deed does not specifically mention that share.

The rule is that “The Partition Law shall not apply to any land or building comprised in any registered Condominium Plan.” Applied to the facts, the land and building are already comprised in a registered Condominium Plan, so the Partition Law does not apply to that property.

Section 13 says that no plan or map, or copy or tracing of a plan or map, is receivable in evidence in any court in Sri Lanka unless it satisfies the statutory preparation and certification requirement.

The provision states one alternative is that the plan or map has been prepared "by or on behalf of the Surveyor-General by a registered surveyor duly authorised by him" and certified "by the Surveyor-General or by a registered surveyor duly authorised by him for such purpose". It also states paragraph (b): "and certified by a registered licensed surveyor."

So, the plan or map must be prepared in the manner stated in section 13 and must be certified in the manner stated there before it can be received in evidence.

Yes. The provision says that any cadastral map, plan, or other plan or map prepared in accordance with any written law, when it purports to be a true copy and to be signed by the Surveyor-General or an officer acting on his behalf, “shall be admissible evidence in all cases and for all purposes instead of the original.” It also “may be taken as prima facie evidence of the truth of the facts stated there in as being that of the original.” 

Applied here, because the party produces a copy purporting to be authenticated and signed by the Surveyor-General, the copy is admissible in place of the original. Its initial evidential status is prima facie evidence of the truth of the facts stated in it, until evidence to the contrary is first given. It is not necessary at that stage to prove that it was in fact signed or authenticated by the Surveyor-General or that it is a true copy.

Under section 73, it is “not… lawful for the company to register a transfer of shares… unless a proper instrument of transfer has been delivered to the company.” On the facts, no proper instrument of transfer has been delivered, so the company may not register the voluntary transfer.

The proviso creates an exception where “the right of any shares… has been transmitted by operation of law.” In that case, nothing in section 73 affects the company’s power to register that person as shareholder.

Under Companies Act, s 79, “A certificate signed under the name of the company by a director and secretary of the company specifying any shares held by any shareholder, shall be prima facie evidence of the title of the shareholder to the shares.” Applied here, a share certificate signed in the company’s name by a director and the secretary is prima facie evidence that the recorded shareholder has title to the shares specified in the certificate.

The director breached these statutory duties:

1. Under Companies Act, s 188, a director “shall not act or agree to the company acting, in a manner that contravenes ... the provisions contained in the articles of the company.” Approving conduct that breaches the company’s articles falls within that prohibition.

2. Under Companies Act, s 189(a), a person exercising powers or performing duties as a director “shall not act in a manner which is reckless or grossly negligent.” Carrying out the decision recklessly breaches that duty.

3. Under Companies Act, s 189(b), a person exercising powers or performing duties as a director “shall exercise the degree of skill and care that may reasonably be expected of a person of his knowledge and experience.” Failing to exercise the reasonably expected skill and care breaches that duty.

The statutory rule is that any “alienation” of land made in contravention of the Act “shall be void and shall have no effect in law.” The Act defines “alienation” to mean a “transfer, lease or mortgage of lands situated within Sri Lanka.” Applying that rule, a transfer of land completed in direct contravention of the Act is void and has no legal effect.
